sections.h: Onias III, Jason and Menelaus in 2 Maccabees
sections.b:
2 Maccabees makes Onias III the model high priest: "the man who did good to the city," protector of his people and zealous for the laws (2 Maccabees 4:2). When Simon the temple officer slanders him, Onias goes to the king for the people's sake (2 Maccabees 4:1–6). Under Antiochus IV his brother Jason buys the office and founds a gymnasium (2 Maccabees 4:7–17); three years later Menelaus, Simon's brother and not of the high priestly line, outbids Jason (2 Maccabees 4:23–26). When Onias exposes Menelaus's theft of temple vessels, Menelaus has Andronicus lure him from the sanctuary at Daphne and kill him, about 170 BC (2 Maccabees 4:32–38). Jason dies an exile among the Spartans (2 Maccabees 5:5–10), and Menelaus keeps office by bribery (2 Maccabees 4:45–50) until his execution (2 Maccabees 13:3–8).

Josephus tells it differently: Jason succeeds a dead Onias, and Menelaus is a third brother, also called Onias (Antiquities 12.237–240). Most historians prefer 2 Maccabees. Many scholars take Daniel's "an anointed one will be cut off" (Daniel 9:26) and "a prince of the covenant" (Daniel 11:22), and the lamb seized in 1 Enoch 90:8, as references to Onias's murder.

common: Onias III was deposed when his brother Jason bought the high priesthood from Antiochus IV about 175 BC.
uncommon: Some historians think Andronicus was executed for murdering Seleucus IV's son, and that 2 Maccabees has linked his death to Onias instead (Diodorus 30.7.2).

sections.b: 2 Maccabees is the first known text to use Hellēnismos for a way of life: under Jason "the Greek way came to its height and foreign ways advanced" (2 Maccabees 4:13), its opposite being "Judaism" (2 Maccabees 2:21). Jason founded a gymnasium and an ephebate below the citadel, enrolled "the Antiochenes in Jerusalem," and put the young men "under the broad-brimmed hat" of Hermes, so that priests left the altar for the wrestling school (2 Maccabees 4:9–15). Under the decree of 167 BC those who would not "switch to the Greek way" were killed (2 Maccabees 6:9), and Eleazar refused to seem to go over to foreign ways (2 Maccabees 6:24). 1 Maccabees 1:11–15 tells the founding of the gymnasium without naming Jason. Scholars debate whether "the Antiochenes" were a new Greek citizen body inside Jerusalem (Bickerman) or the city renamed (Tcherikover).

sections.h: Eleazar, the mother and her seven sons
sections.b: 2 Maccabees 6:18–7:42 holds the most influential martyr stories of the ancient Jewish world. Eleazar, a scribe of ninety, refuses to eat pork or even to pretend, so as not to mislead the young, and dies on the torture frame (2 Maccabees 6:18–31). Seven brothers die one by one before their mother, each confessing the law and the hope of resurrection; then she dies too (2 Maccabees 7:1–41). The youngest calls on God "in me and my brothers to stop the anger of the Almighty" (2 Maccabees 7:37–38), and in the next chapter "the Lord's anger had now turned to mercy" (2 Maccabees 8:5). 4 Maccabees retells the stories at length and calls the deaths "a ransom for the sin of the nation" (4 Maccabees 17:21–22). Hebrews 11:35–36 most likely recalls them. Christians kept their feast from the fourth century, and the Orthodox and the Roman Martyrology keep it on 1 August. The rabbis tell a version under Roman rule (Bavli Gittin 57b; Lamentations Rabbah on Lamentations 1:16).

common: Most commentators think Hebrews 11:35–36 refers to the martyrs of 2 Maccabees 6–7.

sections.b: The brothers of 2 Maccabees 7 give one of the clearest pre-Christian statements of bodily resurrection: "the King of the world will raise us, who died for his laws, to live again forever" (2 Maccabees 7:9); the third hopes to receive back his tongue and hands (2 Maccabees 7:11); the fourth tells the king there will be no "resurrection to life" for him (2 Maccabees 7:14); the mother hopes to receive her sons back "in the mercy to come" (2 Maccabees 7:29), arguing from God's power as Creator (2 Maccabees 7:22–23). Only Daniel 12:2 is as clear before it. The Catholic Catechism cites 2 Maccabees 7:9, 14 and 29 (Catechism 992).

The mother of the seven tells her youngest son that God made the sky and the earth "not from things that were" (2 Maccabees 7:28). The Vulgate rendered it ex nihilo, Origen cited it for creation out of nothing (On First Principles 2.1.5), and the Catholic Catechism quotes it (Catechism 297). Many modern scholars think the verse says less than the later, strict doctrine: Gerhard May finds in it only God's sovereign act of creation, with no rejection of eternal matter, and Jonathan Goldstein (1984) also denied that it teaches creation from nothing. Goldstein's wider claim, that the doctrine arose to defend resurrection, was disputed by David Winston (1986), and Goldstein partly withdrew it (1987). Paul Copan defends the older reading. Wisdom 11:17 speaks of creation "out of formless matter". Latter-day Saints, following Joseph Smith, hold that God organized eternal matter.

2 Maccabees says the king sent an elderly Athenian to make the Jews give up their ancestral laws and to rename the Jerusalem temple for Olympian Zeus and the temple on Gerizim for Zeus, Protector of Guests (2 Maccabees 6:1–2). The courts were filled with revels, and forbidden sacrifices loaded the altar (2 Maccabees 6:4–5). 1 Maccabees 1:54 calls the altar "an abomination of desolation," Daniel's phrase (Daniel 11:31). Many scholars think the god behind "Zeus" was the Syrian Baal Shamem, and that Daniel's shiqquts shomem mocks that name.

The writer of 2 Maccabees stops before the martyr stories to tell his readers that the calamities were "for the correction of our people": God punishes the nations only when their sins are full, but disciplines Israel quickly, so "he never removes his mercy from us" (2 Maccabees 6:12–17). The brothers echo it: "We suffer this because of ourselves" (2 Maccabees 7:18, 32–33). The same teaching is in Deuteronomy 8:5, Proverbs 3:11–12 and Hebrews 12:5–11.

sections.b: 2 Maccabees tells how the high priesthood, held by Onias's family, was bought from Antiochus IV: first by Jason, Onias's brother, for 440 talents, probably each year, and 150 more for his gymnasium (2 Maccabees 4:7–9), then by Menelaus, who was not of the high priestly family, for 300 talents more (2 Maccabees 4:23–24). The writer denies Jason the title, "ungodly and no high priest" (2 Maccabees 4:13). Later the Hasmoneans too received the office from kings (1 Maccabees 10:20).

sections.h: "He chose the place for the sake of the nation"
sections.b: 2 Maccabees explains why God, who struck down Heliodorus at the treasury, let Antiochus IV rob the temple: the people had sinned, and the Lord "did not choose the nation for the sake of the place; he chose the place for the sake of the nation" (2 Maccabees 5:17–20). The temple shared the people's disaster and, when God was reconciled, their glory (2 Maccabees 10:1–8). Compare Jeremiah 7:4–14.

2 Maccabees likes fitting punishments. The Hellenizers are punished by the Greeks they envied (2 Maccabees 4:16); Andronicus is executed where he killed Onias (2 Maccabees 4:38); the temple robber Lysimachus dies by the treasury (2 Maccabees 4:42); Jason, who left many unburied and drove many into exile, dies an exile and unburied (2 Maccabees 5:9–10).

2 Maccabees explains the persecution as God's brief anger at his people's sins. The Master "had grown angry for a short while" (2 Maccabees 5:17); God punishes Israel quickly so that its sins do not reach their full measure, as the nations' do (2 Maccabees 6:12–16); the youngest brother says the living Lord "has become angry for a short time" and will make peace again (2 Maccabees 7:33), and calls on God to stop his anger in the brothers' deaths (2 Maccabees 7:37–38). When Judas gathers his men, "the Lord's anger had now turned to mercy" (2 Maccabees 8:5). The pattern follows Isaiah 54:7–8.
